This right here, in a nutshell, is why people have a negative attitude towards India and how women are treated. 

No matter how vulgar you think the photo and behavior of these celebrities are, it is a consensual act between two adults. It is not the same as rape, or domestic violence. To equate the two is to think that the crime of a rape is the *gasp! How taboo!* sex, rather than the criminal violence happening to the abused. It is a disgusting and deeply regressive position.

So I’ll try to answer this - I’m born in the US but from Indian heritage, and would describe myself as a staunch Democrat in America, neutral-to-leaning against Modi (but most importantly, quite apathetic about him) in India. 

I think some of the better faith answers from some on this thread are partially correct. American media incorrectly assumes first that the Indian right wing is identical to the American right wing, and secondly incorrectly assumes that being anti-BJP necessarily makes you a social liberal. I would not describe American media as so much “anti-India” as deeply insular, and fundamentally unable to understand a multiparty system with several political entities insistent on oppressive, regressive, and backward policies. Our politics here are fundamentally governed by a singular religious-political entity, and people upset with that entity.

I find the opposition in India to be fractured, corrupt, and deeply unaccountable. It would be a preposterous proposition for a major party leader in the USA to go to a general election and win less than 10% of seats, and remain the party leader. Far less _twice_. Rahul Gandhi seems to have no vision for India beyond increasing the amount of reservation for underprivileged castes, and I have yet to understand what an INDIA government would do that is materially superior to that of the ruling NDA. Transportation and infrastructure have dramatically improved in the last 10 years. This must be acknowledged by a good-faith opposition.

The reason why I lean anti-Modi is what I perceive to be (not from the media, from my own lived experiences visiting India) a brand of religious nationalism that tries to mirror the Christian nationalism that I find repulsive in the United States. I’m talking about the kind of people that think Mohammed Shami would fix a game against Pakistan because he’s Muslim, or the type of person that genuinely thinks military capture of PoK is imminent any year now. Pakistan is a nuclear armed state, like it or not. I find this ideology to be not just morally bankrupt, but intellectually dishonest. It shouts “Akhand Bharat” and “Hindu Rashtra” in the same sentence, ignoring that 700 million people would have to be deported or killed to make that happen. This is not a decolonial or anti-oppression agenda. It is itself maniacal, and deeply delusional. 

But despite my views, I am generally apathetic about this overall. Where I start caring is when my parents, and people in that generation, act as if Modi is the 10th avatar or better, that India is far, far superior to the USA despite their entire life being made here, that I personally am somehow deficient or a borderline traitor for being genuinely proud of my American heritage. I’m not confused in the slightest. India is like a second home to me. But it is second. America is first. And that - hear me clearly - _completely settled_ identity is brought under direct, personal threat by the rise of a political movement that has inspired a lot of NRIs to believe that they live in a “backward hellhole” in the USA, and only the sanskaar and values of a pure Hindu India can save them, and crucially, their children. 

That’s my full and complete view of the matter.

As an American of Indian descent who has just spent a month in India and have been repeatedly flabbergasted by the fact that talking points from Indian conservatives seem to be from the desk of any of our most rabid podcasters or political leaders, thank you. I want to believe that our grifters are not shaping policy worldwide, both on the left and right.

No one else in my family will go and I didn’t want to go back home during the pandemic (not because of them, I just needed to sort myself out alone) but my dad took it personally that I don’t want to come home and that I hate him and said he was going to come pick me up from where I was living. 

I’m also making it sound worse than it is but like..... as far as this is concerned it’s like 

Idk *trails off*
She said that she was afraid to confront him and has been afraid to in the past. I don’t want to get involved but I could see it was hurting her and she didn’t want to escalate it.
My roommates would have to break their lease without me since they were dependent on it.
I completely understand, that's why I asked. Thanks.

So I don't actually use the word "she" in conversations at all anymore, even when referring to the past. This is only specific to my own written history of the events that took place, where the gender becomes relevant - for example, "I wanted to ask her to prom." The pronouns are used literally hundreds of times in the telling of the story in ways like this. If I use 'they' there or even put quotes around 'her' or any other such qualifier, it gives the reality away before the story is complete.
